vignette:
She is twenty and has been working as an auditor for just over a year when the stalking begins to reshape her life. At first, it feels like a series of unsettling coincidences: a car she notices twice outside her apartment, a message request from an unfamiliar account, a man who seems to know which café she prefers near the office. She tells herself she is being overly cautious, that the pace of adult life in the city has made everyone a little suspicious. As an auditor, she is trained to notice inconsistencies and patterns, yet in her own life she keeps trying to explain away the small disturbances. She does not want to seem dramatic. She does not want to be the person who overreacts.

The attention becomes harder to dismiss when it starts to follow her routines. A parcel is left at her building with no sender. She sees her name written in a hand she does not recognize. Once, walking home from work, she realizes someone is behind her for several blocks, keeping pace when she slows and slowing when she does. After that she begins changing her route, checking reflections in shop windows, pausing before entering her street so she can scan for familiar cars. She starts arriving at work with a tightness in her chest already in place, as though her body has learned fear before her mind has fully caught up.

Her colleagues notice that she becomes quieter in meetings. She used to be neat, efficient, almost exacting with her files, but now she double-checks doors, hesitates before using the lift, and keeps her phone face down on her desk. She sits with her back to the wall in lunchrooms and feels foolish for doing so. The stalking makes ordinary spaces feel contaminated. Her apartment, once private and restful, no longer gives her the sense of safety it should. She keeps lights on longer than she needs to. She puts a chair against the bedroom door some nights, then lies awake angry at herself for being afraid in her own home.

The fear soon settles into her body. She startles at footsteps in the hallway. Her sleep becomes light and fractured, full of waking and checking. When she does sleep, she dreams of being watched from across streets, from behind windows, from the darkened back seat of a car. She wakes sweating, with her heart racing, and spends minutes listening for sounds outside her door. During the day she is increasingly tired and on edge, and her concentration at work suffers. She rereads audit reports because her mind drifts after a sentence or two. Numbers that once felt orderly now blur when she is exhausted, and she worries that someone will notice she is not performing with her usual precision.

She begins to avoid places that once felt ordinary and enjoyable. She stops going to the gym after work. She takes longer, more complicated routes to get home. She declines invitations from friends because she does not want to explain why she is looking over her shoulder all the time, and because being out in public feels like leaving herself exposed. When her phone buzzes unexpectedly, she flinches before she can stop herself. She deletes photos that show her in familiar places. She changes passwords, then changes them again. Even these precautions do not bring relief; instead, they reinforce the sense that danger is close and persistent.

What troubles her most is how alone the experience makes her feel. She says she has become less like herself, more guarded and less trusting, as if a part of her is always braced for the next sign that he is still there. She feels shame for the intensity of her fear, and then guilt for feeling ashamed, as though she should be able to do what she has always done at work: gather the facts, stay composed, move through the problem. But the stalking has not behaved like a problem she can solve by being careful enough. It has entered her thoughts, her body, and her sense of the world. Even now, she scans parking lots before unlocking her car and listens for a second set of footsteps when she walks alone, carrying on with daily life while constantly measuring how safe she is allowed to feel.
